To keep a literal path to its own methods, give it routes for the others.
- Middleware layered on a nested router run for its routes, and for what giong-web answers by itself for its paths: the automatic `OPTIONS` (CORS preflights included, through the middleware of the route the preflight asks about) and the `405` for a path of one of its routes, and the `404` for a path under its prefix. So `Cors` can be layered on the router nested at `/api`.
- `/users` and `/users/` are different paths. giong-web does not redirect from one to the other; its `404` names the one that exists.
- `req.route()` gives the pattern that matched (`/teams/{team}/members/{id}`), for logs and metrics.
- `Router::route(method, pattern, handler)` takes any method; `get`, `post`, `put`, `patch` and `delete` are shortcuts.
- There is no `merge`. To keep the routes under one prefix in several routers (public ones and ones behind a key, say), `nest` each of them at the same prefix: `.nest("/api", public).nest("/api", private)`. Each keeps its own middleware; a `404` under the prefix goes through the first one's.

## Errors

```json
{"status":400,"code":"GIONG-E1205","title":"Bad Request","detail":"path parameter `id`: cannot read \"abc\" (invalid digit found in string); expected an unsigned integer","request_id":"3f9a0c1e7d2b4a59000200000000002a"}
```

| Status | Code | When |
|---|---|---|
| 404 | `GIONG-E1203` | no route for the path |
| 405 | `GIONG-E1204` | the path has routes, not for this method; `Allow` lists them |
| 400 | `GIONG-E1205` | a path or query parameter that does not parse |
| 500 | `GIONG-E1206` | the handler asked for a parameter its route does not have (a bug: the cause names the route) |
| 400, 422 | `GIONG-E1207` | a JSON body that is not JSON (`400`) or does not fit the type (`422`) |
| 415 | `GIONG-E1208` | a body that should be JSON and has another `Content-Type` |
| 503 | `GIONG-E1209` | `Timeout` ran out |
| 500 | `GIONG-E1210` | the handler failed, or a handler or middleware panicked; the cause is logged, never sent |
| 503 | `GIONG-E1211` | a database or service the handler needs cannot be reached (giong's connect, timeout and pool errors); `Retry-After: 1`. A statement the database cancelled at its own statement timeout (`GIONG-E3004`) is not among them: it is a `500` |
| 403 | `GIONG-E1212` | a CORS preflight that `Cors` refused, saying which of origin, method or header |

Your own errors take your own codes: `Error::not_found("user_not_found", "no user 42")`, `Error::conflict(..)`, `Error::new(429, "rate_limited", ..).with_header("Retry-After", "30")`. `Error::new` and `with_header` panic on a status outside `400..=599` and on a header value with a control character, which suits literals; a status or a value that comes from elsewhere goes through `Error::from_status` (anything else becomes `502`, the status given logged) and `try_with_header` (`Err` gives the error back without the header). `Error::of(&response)` reads the error back from a response, for middleware and tests. Every error response has `Cache-Control: no-store`.

**Not problem+json: what `giong-http` refuses before the app sees the request.** A body larger than the server's `max_body_size` (`413`; 1 MiB unless changed, so a large JSON `POST` is enough), a head larger than its limit (`431`) and a request that is not valid HTTP (`400`) are answered by the server below giong-web: the status with an empty body, no code, no `X-Request-Id`, and no line from `Logger` or `Trace`, since no middleware runs. A client should read a `4xx` without a body as one of these three. The same goes for a request refused because the worker already holds as many request bytes as the server's `max_buffered_request_bytes` allows: `503` with `Retry-After: 1` and a plain-text body that starts with `GIONG-E1120` (over HTTP/2 the stream is refused with `REFUSED_STREAM` instead); retry it. On a route with `stream_bodies`, a body announced as longer than the route's limit is refused before the handler runs, the same bare way; one that grows past the limit while the handler reads it is a problem+json `413` (`GIONG-E1111`).

`?` finds a giong code anywhere down the error's `source()` chain, so a pool timeout wrapped in your own error type is still a `503`. It reads the code from the type of giong's errors and from the start of the companion crates' messages, never from the text of an `io::Error`.

## Middleware

```rust
use giong_web::{Error, Middleware, Next, Req, Response};

struct RequireAuth;
struct UserId(u64);

impl<S: 'static> Middleware<S> for RequireAuth {
    async fn call(&self, mut req: Req<S>, next: Next<'_, S>) -> Result<Response, Error> {
        match req.header_str("authorization") {
            Some(token) if token.starts_with("Bearer ") => {
                req.set_extension(UserId(42)); // the handler reads req.extension::<UserId>()
                Ok(next.run(req).await)
            }
            _ => Err(Error::unauthorized("no_token", "send a bearer token")
                .with_header("WWW-Authenticate", "Bearer")),
        }
    }
}
```

`next.run(req)` returns the `Response`, with an error from further in already turned into its problem+json answer, so a middleware sees and can change every response. The first layer added is the outermost, the reverse of axum's `Router::layer` (where the last one added is): code ported from axum lists its layers the other way round. Add them in this order, outermost first:

| Middleware | What it does | Defaults |
|---|---|---|
| `RequestId::new()` | gives every request an id (`req.request_id()`) and sends it back in `X-Request-Id` | ids made here; an incoming one is used only with `.trust_incoming(true)` |
| `Logger::new(Sink::Stdout)` | one JSON line per request: time, method, path, route, status, duration, bytes, request id, peer, worker, and for errors the code, detail and cause | query strings left out (`.include_query(true)`); written by a background thread, never on the worker |
| `Cors::new()` | answers preflights and adds `Access-Control-Allow-*` for the origins named; on the outermost router or a nested one, before any credentials check (preflights carry none) | no origin allowed until named with `.allow_origin(..)`; methods `GET`, `HEAD`, `POST`; no extra headers |
| `Compression::new()` | gzip for clients that accept it | level 1, bodies from 1 KiB to 16 MiB; text, JSON, JavaScript, XML (SVG too) and WebAssembly |
| `Timeout::new(d)` | answers `503` (`GIONG-E1209`) when the handler takes longer than `d` | not for routes that stream their request body |
| `Trace::new()` (feature `tracing`) | runs each request in a `tracing` span with OpenTelemetry's field names (`http.request.method`, `url.path`, `http.route`, `http.response.status_code`, `client.address`) plus `request_id` and `worker`, ended by one event; a `5xx` at `ERROR` with its code and cause | instead of `Logger`, or beside it |

A log line:

```json
{"ts":"2026-11-13T09:21:04.118302Z","level":"info","event":"request","method":"GET","path":"/users/42","route":"/users/{id}","status":200,"duration_us":84,"bytes":51,"request_id":"3f9a0c1e7d2b4a59000200000000002a","peer":"10.0.0.7:51122","worker":2}
```

A request dropped before its response is ready (the client reset its HTTP/2 stream, or a `Timeout` layered outside the logger gave up) gets a line too, at the drop, with `"event":"request cancelled"`, `"status":null` and the time until then; `Trace` ends its span with a `request cancelled` event.

The log thread batches lines every 10 ms. When it falls behind by more than 1 MiB per worker, lines are dropped and counted in a `log_dropped` line, instead of the workers waiting or memory growing. Once written, a worker's buffer shrinks back to 64 KiB, and a thread's buffer goes when the thread ends. A path or query string longer than 4 KiB is cut, ending `...(+N bytes)`. `giong_web::flush_logs()` waits for what is queued (up to 2 s); dropping an `App` calls it.

## Streaming

```rust
use giong_web::{Body, Error, Req, Response, Router};

async fn upload(req: Req) -> Result<Response, Error> {
    // Checked by `param`: no `..` or `.` segment, no NUL, not absolute.
    let name: String = req.param("path")?;
    let body = req.body_stream().expect("a streaming route");
    let mut total = 0;
    while let Some(piece) = body.chunk().await? {
        total += piece.len(); // write it under the uploads directory, hash it, ...
    }
    Ok(Response::text(format!("{name}: {total} bytes")))
}

async fn events(_req: Req) -> Result<Response, Error> {
    let (tx, body) = Body::channel();
    drop(giong::spawn(async move {
        for n in 0.. {
            if tx.send(format!("data: {n}\n\n")).await.is_err() {
                break; // the client went away
            }
            giong::time::sleep(std::time::Duration::from_secs(1)).await;
        }
    }));
    Ok(Response::new(200).header("Content-Type", "text/event-stream").body(body))
}

let uploads = Router::new().put("/files/{*path}", upload).stream_bodies(10 << 30);
let app = Router::new().get("/events", events).nest("/api", uploads).build(());
```

- `stream_bodies(max)` applies to every route of its router, wherever the router is nested. Other routes still get their body in full, within the server's `max_body_size`.
- Nothing of the body is read until the handler asks, so a handler can refuse an upload (no credentials, no space) before the client sends it. One piece is in flight at a time: a slow handler slows the client down instead of filling memory.
- `?` on a body error answers `413` (`GIONG-E1111`, past `max`) or `400` (`GIONG-E1112` cut short, `GIONG-E1113` malformed). A body announced past `max` gets `413` before the handler runs. `req.json()` on a streaming route is a `500` whose logged cause says to read the stream.
- `Timeout` does not limit a streaming route, whose handler runs while the body arrives; each piece still has the server's `request_timeout`. Work done once the body is in (a database call, an upstream request) needs its own limit: wrap it in `giong::time::timeout` (the `Timeout` docs show how). `Compression` leaves streamed responses alone, and `Logger` writes `"bytes":null` for them.
- A streamed response goes out chunked, each piece as soon as it is sent. `send` fails once the client has gone (noticed at the next write), so the producer stops.

## Testing

```rust
use giong_web::{Error, Req, Request, Response, Router};

async fn get_user(req: Req<()>) -> Result<Response, Error> {
    let id: u64 = req.param("id")?;
    Ok(Response::text(format!("user {id}")))
}

let app = Router::new().get("/users/{id}", get_user).build(());
let req = Request::from_bytes(b"GET /users/abc HTTP/1.1\r\nHost: t\r\n\r\n").unwrap();
let resp = giong::block_on(app.handle(req));
assert_eq!(resp.status(), 400);
assert_eq!(giong_web::Error::of(&resp).unwrap().code(), "GIONG-E1205");
```

## Performance

Measured with `bench/web.sh`: the same handlers on giong-web and on axum 0.8.9 (Tokio 1.54, hyper 1.12), both with serde_json 1.0, each server on one core and `wrk` on another of a 4-vCPU virtual machine (Xeon 2.1 GHz, Linux 6.18), 50 connections. `/json` serializes a one-field struct, `/users` a list of 100 users (8 KB), `/users/{id}` reads a path parameter, `/compute?n=25` a typed query and then computes a Fibonacci number. The middleware rows add request ids, gzip at level 1 from 1 KiB and a 10 s timeout: giong-web's own, and tower-http 0.6.11's for axum; `wrk` asks for gzip. Requests per second, median of 5 interleaved rounds of 5 s, with the range; p99 is the median of the rounds' p99s.

| | `/json` | p99 | `/users` | p99 | `/users/{id}` | `/compute` | Pipelined `/json` |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **giong-web** | **152.5k** (147–187k) | **0.93 ms** | **28.0k** (25–31k) | **3.9 ms** | **140.5k** (124–162k) | 3.7k | **804k** |
| axum | 118.3k (111–141k) | 1.26 ms | 15.2k (14–16k) | 5.3 ms | 107.1k (74–124k) | 3.9k | 18k |
| giong-http, a bare handler | 160.4k (159–168k) | 0.81 ms | 48.3k (43–51k) | 2.6 ms | | 3.5k | 1.16M |

With middleware:

| | `/json` | p99 | `/users`, gzip | p99 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **giong-web** | **126.2k** (124–133k) | **1.04 ms** | **12.0k** (11.2–12.2k) | **7.9 ms** |
| axum + tower-http | 65.8k (59–75k) | 1.91 ms | 5.2k (4.6–5.9k) | 13.6 ms |

- **1.3 times axum on small JSON answers, 1.8 times on the list of users, 1.9 to 2.3 times with middleware.** The routes, the parameters and serde cost giong-web about 5% against giong-http's bare handler on `/json`. giong-http's `/users` is faster because it writes its JSON by hand, without serde or the 200 small strings the handler builds; giong-web and axum run the same handler.
- **`/compute` is the handler's time,** the same for both within noise (giong-web's range 3.66–4.01k, axum's 3.58–4.07k). Its p99 is higher on giong-web (22.9 against 18.5 ms), as it is on giong-http (24.2 ms). Our guess, not measured: a worker runs every ready request before it reads its sockets again, so when each costs 250 µs of CPU, some wait for a whole batch.
- **Pipelined requests** (16 per write): axum stays at 18k, as in the [main benchmark](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.0.0-rc.1/README.md#throughput-at-50-connections); we have not looked into why. giong-http reads a pipeline and answers it as a batch.
- Resident memory after the run: 6.6 MB for giong-web, 5.2 MB for axum.

HTTPS and a database behind the handlers are measured with the [example REST API](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.0.0-rc.1/examples/rest-api/README.md#performance). Not measured yet: several cores, and middleware one at a time. Results are in `bench/results/web/`.

## Features

| Feature | Adds |
|---|---|
| `serde` | `req.json::<T>()`, `req.query::<T>()` and `json(status, &value)`, through serde and serde_json |
| `tls` | `Server::serve_tls`, through giong-http: HTTP/2 or HTTP/1.1, as ALPN picks |
| `tracing` | `middleware::Trace`, through `tracing` 0.1 |

Apps are served over HTTP/2 as well as HTTP/1.1, with nothing to change: giong-http turns each HTTP/2 stream into the request a handler already knows (see [its HTTP/2 section](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.0.0-rc.1/giong-http/README.md#http2)). Over TLS, ALPN picks the protocol; without TLS, a client that knows the server speaks HTTP/2 (prior knowledge) gets it on the same port.

## Not there yet

Cookies and sessions, forms and multipart bodies, WebSockets, serving static files, and compressions other than gzip. The crate has had no independent security audit.

## Tests

`cargo test -p giong-web --all-features`: 36 tests without a socket, most through `App::handle`: text beating parameters beating catch-alls, `HEAD`, `404` with its hint, `405` and `OPTIONS` with `Allow` (the union of every route that matches the path), parameters that do not parse and a parameter the route lacks, `..`, `.`, NUL and `%2F` refused in parameters, query strings, errors from `?`, state and nested routers, the order middleware run in and which routes they see, the router's own `404`, `405` and `OPTIONS` answers passing through a nested router's middleware, a middleware answering by itself and passing values to the handler, closures, the startup panics for bad and duplicate routes; a panicking handler or middleware answered `500` and logged once; request ids (made, trusted only when asked, sent back), log lines and their fields, long paths cut in them, a line for a request dropped before its response, timeouts, CORS preflights allowed and refused and simple requests, on the outermost router and a nested one, every middleware setting that cannot work, gzip and when not to use it, `HEAD` with the headers of `GET`; JSON bodies in and out, `415`, `400` and `422`, escaped strings and the `500` for a `&str` field that cannot borrow, typed queries, a repeated key and a bad escape refused by both query APIs. 4 tests over real TCP with giong-http's client, over HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2: gzip on the wire for `GET` and `HEAD`, CORS, `405`, 50 requests on one kept-alive connection; a panic that leaves the connection, and the other HTTP/2 streams, alone. 5 tests of streamed bodies over real TCP: uploads past the server's body limit on a streaming route, `413` with its code for one past the route's limit, a slow upload that the timeout leaves alone, `req.json()` on a streaming route, a streamed response that passes through every middleware untouched. 3 tests of `Trace` with a recording subscriber: the span's fields, the code and cause of errors, and the event for a request dropped before its response. 42 unit tests, among them 30,000 random route sets matched against a slow reference matcher (which works out `Allow` its own way), 4,000 random requests through every middleware with the checks below, bodies around the 64 KiB compression slice, giong codes found down an error's `source()` chain, a cause said once when an error already shows its source, and the log writer giving back memory and the slot of a thread that ended. 19 documentation examples.

Two fuzz targets in `fuzz/` (`cargo +nightly fuzz run request`, or `routes`): `routes` checks that the route table finds the route a slow reference finds, with the same parameters, or the same `404`, `405` or `OPTIONS` answer; `request` sends any bytes as a request to an app with every middleware and checks that the answer is well formed: a valid status and headers, a problem+json body with a code for every error, gzip only when asked and decoding to what the handler wrote, one log line that is JSON and agrees with the response, and the request id sent back. 5.4 million inputs ran without a failure when the crate was added; CI fuzzes both every night.

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.0.0-rc.1/giong-mcp/README.md -->

# giong-mcp

An [MCP](https://modelcontextprotocol.io) server that lets an AI agent look inside a running [giong](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.0.0-rc.1/README.md) service: what each worker is doing, which tasks are alive and which line spawned them, what the connection pools hold, and where the time goes. Read-only, on a loopback address or a Unix socket, and only when the service turns it on.

```toml
[dependencies]
giong = "1.0.0-rc.1"
giong-mcp = "1.0.0-rc.1"
```

```rust,no_run
fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> {
    let rt = giong::Builder::new().shutdown_on_signals(true).build()?;
    // Starts only when GIONG_MCP is set. Keep the value: dropping it stops
    // the server.
    let _mcp = giong_mcp::start_from_env(&rt.handle());
    rt.run(|_worker| async {
        // ... the service ...
        giong::shutdown_signal().await;
    })
}
```

```sh
export GIONG_MCP=127.0.0.1:7777 GIONG_MCP_TOKEN=$(openssl rand -hex 16)
cargo run --release
# Claude Code, in another shell with the same GIONG_MCP_TOKEN:
claude mcp add --transport http giong http://127.0.0.1:7777/mcp \
    --header "Authorization: Bearer $GIONG_MCP_TOKEN"
```

Any MCP client that speaks the Streamable HTTP transport works the same way; give it the token as an `Authorization: Bearer` header (in MCP Inspector, the "Bearer Token" field). Without that header a client gets `401`, and some clients then try OAuth discovery and fail with a `404` that does not say why: the header is the fix.

`start_from_env` writes one line to stderr, `giong-mcp: listening on http://127.0.0.1:7777/mcp`, or the coded error that kept the server from starting: a busy port or a bad `GIONG_MCP` leaves the service running without the endpoint, since a debugging aid should not decide whether the service starts. For a JSON log line instead, or to stop the service when the endpoint cannot start, use `Config` and log the result yourself:

```rust,no_run
fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> {
    let rt = giong::Builder::new().shutdown_on_signals(true).build()?;
    // Kept for as long as the service runs, like `_mcp` above.
    let mcp = giong_mcp::Config::from_env()?
        .map(|cfg| cfg.start(&rt.handle()))
        .transpose()?; // a coded error, such as GIONG-E1303, stops the service
    if let Some(mcp) = &mcp {
        // log mcp.url() (None on a Unix socket) your way
        let _ = mcp.url();
    }
    rt.run(|_worker| async {
        // ... the service ...
        giong::shutdown_signal().await;
    })
}
```

In code, `giong_mcp::Config::tcp("127.0.0.1:7777").token(secret).start(&handle)` does the same as the environment variables, and `Config::unix(path)` listens on a Unix socket.

## What an agent can ask

| Tool | Answers |
|---|---|
| `overview` | The process (resident memory, threads, open descriptors against the limit, uptime), the runtime (workers, shutdown, profiling), each worker's state, I/O driver, live tasks, busy share and polls per second over the last second, and warnings. |
| `workers` | Each worker in detail: counters since start (event-loop turns, polls, sleeps, idle time, spawned tasks), rates over the last second, timers, I/O operations in flight, receive buffers, draining, and the task a blocked worker is stuck in. |
| `tasks` | Live tasks grouped by the line that spawned them, across workers or for one (`worker`, `limit`). A count that keeps growing at one line is a leak. |
| `sources` | What registered sources report, summed over workers and per worker: giong-postgres, giong-mysql and giong-redis pools (open, taken, connecting, in flight, waiting, opened, connect errors, timeouts) and anything registered with `giong::observe::register`. |
| `profile` | Times every task poll for `duration_ms` (100 to 10,000, default 1,000), then lists the spawn locations the workers spent their time in: polls, total, share of the window, mean and longest poll. |

The answer that matters most is the one other tools cannot give: **which task blocks a worker.** giong runs many tasks on one thread, so a task that calls a blocking function or computes for a long time without `.await` stalls every other task on its worker. The server samples each worker ten times a second; a worker that is awake but has not moved on is reported with the spawn location of the task it is in:

```json
"warnings": [
  "worker 1 has been inside one poll of the task spawned at src/routes/report.rs:88:13 for 2.3 s: that task blocks the thread (a blocking call, a long computation or a loop without .await), and every other task on worker 1 waits"
]
```

In a giong-http or giong-web service, request handlers run inside the task giong-http spawns for each connection, so a blocking handler is reported as a giong-http connection's task (a location in giong-http's `src/server.rs`), and the warning says so: giong cannot yet name the handler or route. `profile` counts the time of every handler the same way, under that location.

The server runs on a thread and a single-worker giong runtime of its own, so it answers even when every worker of the service is stuck. A worker that cannot answer within `snapshot_timeout` (500 ms by default) is reported as such, with what its counters say.

## How it works

The runtime keeps the data; this crate only serves it. In `giong`:

- Every worker publishes counters and the spawn location of the task it is polling, on a cache line of its own, with relaxed stores: `Handle::pulse(worker)` reads them from any thread without disturbing the worker. That costs about nine instructions per task poll (two of them stores; counted with callgrind on tasks that only yield) and one store per turn of the event loop.
- `spawn`, `Handle::spawn_on` and `Handle::spawn_balanced` record where they were called (`#[track_caller]`), so a task is named by a line of your code, and `observe::snapshot()` groups the live tasks by it.
- `Handle::set_profiling(true)` makes every worker read the clock around each poll; when it is off, it costs one relaxed load per batch of tasks (the loop is compiled twice, with and without the clock).
- Pools register themselves as `observe::Source`s, by weak reference.

## Security

Whoever can reach the server can read the internals of the service: task locations, pool addresses (never user names or passwords), memory figures. So:

- It listens on `127.0.0.1`, `::1` or a Unix socket, and refuses any other address with [GIONG-E1301](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.0.0-rc.1/docs/errors/E1301.md). To reach a service elsewhere, forward the port (`ssh -L 7777:127.0.0.1:7777 host`, `kubectl port-forward`).
- On TCP, every request needs `Authorization: Bearer <token>` (`GIONG_MCP_TOKEN`, `Config::token`): every process on the machine can connect to a loopback port, whichever user runs it, and so can every container in the same pod. Without a token the server does not start ([GIONG-E1304](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.0.0-rc.1/docs/errors/E1304.md)), unless the code opts out with `Config::allow_unauthenticated()`, for a development machine. A token must be at least 16 characters a bearer token can carry; an empty one is refused rather than taken to mean "no token" ([GIONG-E1305](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.0.0-rc.1/docs/errors/E1305.md)).
- A Unix socket is created with mode `0600`, under a temporary name first, so that it is never reachable by other users, and needs no token. A live socket at the path is never replaced, and stopping removes only the socket this server created. Most MCP clients speak HTTP over TCP only; to use one with a socket, bridge it: `socat TCP-LISTEN:7777,bind=127.0.0.1,fork UNIX-CONNECT:/run/giong/mcp.sock` (which lets every local process in again), or `ssh -L 7777:/run/giong/mcp.sock host` from another machine.
- A request whose `Host` header is not a loopback name, or whose `Origin` is not a loopback origin, is refused with `403`: a web page cannot reach the server through DNS rebinding.
- What a client can make the server hold is bounded, since it lives in the service's process. Requests are served over HTTP/1.1 only (an HTTP/2 connection could carry a hundred at once), on at most 16 connections, each answered one request at a time; more wait in the kernel's listen queue. A body holds at most 64 KiB (`413` past that), a batch at most 16 messages, and an answer at most 4 MiB (an error past that, which tells the agent to ask for less). Connections idle for 60 s are closed, and a request must arrive within 10 s. Before these limits, 24 connections each sending one 254 KiB batch took a 4-worker service from 4 MB to 2 GB; now 64 such connections leave it under 8 MB.
- The tools only read, apart from `profile`, which makes every worker time its polls for the window it measures (its `readOnlyHint` is false, so clients can ask before calling it). It shares the runtime's profiling switch with the service: it is refused while the service has profiling on, and it discards poll timings the service collected earlier and has not taken yet.

## Protocol

MCP over Streamable HTTP at `/mcp`, protocol versions 2025-11-25, 2025-06-18 and 2025-03-26. One JSON-RPC message per `POST`, answered with `application/json`; notifications and the client's responses get `202 Accepted`. Batches (at most 16 messages) are answered only for clients of 2025-03-26, the one version that has them; a request with a later `MCP-Protocol-Version` gets `-32600`. The server offers no event stream (`GET` gets `405`) and keeps no sessions.

Tool results carry the JSON both as `structuredContent` and as compact text, and each tool declares the shape of its answer as an `outputSchema`, so clients can validate answers and models know the fields before the first call. That JSON is part of the crate's API: from 1.0 on, fields are added in minor releases and never renamed, retyped or removed before 2.0. Fields that are present only in some answers (a worker that did not answer, a call for one worker) are marked so in the schema.

## Testing

`cargo test -p giong-mcp`: 34 tests. Fourteen run a two-worker service with a server on a loopback port and a plain HTTP client: the handshake and tool list, every tool's answer checked against known tasks and sources and against its `outputSchema`, a service with nothing to do reported as idle, a worker blocked in `std::thread::sleep` reported with its line while the other worker still answers, a panicking source told apart from a stopped worker, a profile finding a busy task, JSON-RPC errors and malformed messages, the limits (the review's 254 KiB batch, batches past 16 or from newer clients, 24 clients at once with the process's memory checked), the token rules, busy addresses, and the refusals (token, `Host`, `Origin`, method, content type, protocol version, non-loopback addresses, a Unix socket's mode, a stale socket replaced and a live one or a successor's left alone). `tests/env.rs` checks that `start_from_env` keeps the service running whatever goes wrong. Sixteen unit tests cover address parsing, tokens, a listener the kernel put somewhere else than asked, the `Host` check and the `Bearer` scheme, version negotiation, the watcher (including a second-long window under quick calls), `/proc`, a `profile` call dropped half-way (profiling goes back off), giong-http's connection tasks told apart from others and the fuzz target's starting inputs; three doc tests check the example and that dropping the server at once is a warning. `tests/observe.rs` in the runtime (10 tests) checks the counters, spawn locations, profiles and sources underneath, on both drivers.

`fuzz/` has a cargo-fuzz target, `request`, that sends any bytes as one request through every check and the JSON-RPC dispatch, and checks that the answer is one the server means to send and that no request without the token gets through (`cd giong-mcp && cargo +nightly fuzz run request`).

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.0.0-rc.1/giong-compat/README.md -->

# giong-compat

The I/O traits of Tokio and of the futures crates for [giong](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.0.0-rc.1/README.md)'s streams, so that protocol crates which are generic over their transport run on giong: TLS (tokio-rustls, futures-rustls), WebSocket (tokio-tungstenite), HTTP/2 (h2), hyper's connection API, framing (tokio-util's codecs) and the like. No Tokio runtime is involved: giong drives everything, on its own threads.

```toml
[dependencies]
giong = "1.0.0-rc.1"
giong-compat = "1.0.0-rc.1"
```

```rust,no_run
use giong::net::TcpStream;
use giong_compat::Compat;
use tokio::io::{AsyncReadExt, AsyncWriteExt};

fn main() -> std::io::Result<()> {
    giong::block_on(async {
        let mut stream = Compat::new(TcpStream::connect("127.0.0.1:7000").await?);
        stream.write_all(b"ping\n").await?;
        stream.flush().await?; // writes are buffered until a flush, or until a read waits
        let mut reply = [0; 5];
        stream.read_exact(&mut reply).await?;
        Ok(())
    })
}
```

`Compat<S>` wraps a `giong::net::TcpStream`, a `giong::net::UnixStream` or, with the `tls` feature, a `giong_tls::TlsStream`, and implements `AsyncRead`, `AsyncWrite` and `AsyncBufRead` from `tokio::io` (feature `tokio`) and from `futures_io` (feature `futures-io`). Both features are on by default and pull in the trait definitions only: `tokio` with its default features off, so no runtime, reactor or timer. The libraries build on Rust 1.80.

## When to use it, and when not

**Use the giong crate when there is one; `Compat` is the bridge for a protocol giong has no crate for yet.** The giong crates are built on giong's owned buffers and batched system calls, and measured against the Tokio crates they replace on Tokio they serve 1.1 to 5.1 times the requests or statements per core on the workloads measured, with the exceptions listed there ([the table in giong's README](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.0.0-rc.1/README.md#choosing-crates)). A Tokio crate run on giong through `Compat` keeps its own design and adds the copies described under [What it costs](#what-it-costs). No crate over `Compat` has been measured against the giong crate for the same protocol.

| You need | Use |
|---|---|
| An HTTP/1.1 or HTTP/2 server or client (not hyper or reqwest) | [`giong-http`](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.0.0-rc.1/giong-http/README.md); [`giong-web`](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.0.0-rc.1/giong-web/README.md) for routing and JSON |
| TLS (tokio-rustls over `Compat` works too, with `Compat`'s copies added) | [`giong-tls`](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.0.0-rc.1/giong-tls/README.md) |
| PostgreSQL, MySQL, Redis (not sqlx, tokio-postgres or redis-rs, which need the Tokio runtime) | [`giong-postgres`](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.0.0-rc.1/giong-postgres/README.md), [`giong-mysql`](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.0.0-rc.1/giong-mysql/README.md), [`giong-redis`](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.0.0-rc.1/giong-redis/README.md) |
| h2's own API (HTTP/2 frames and streams, or a library built on h2) | [h2](https://docs.rs/h2) over `Compat`, plain or over `giong-tls` with ALPN `h2` |
| WebSocket | [tokio-tungstenite](https://docs.rs/tokio-tungstenite) (`accept_async`, `client_async`) over `Compat` |
| A protocol framed by length or by line | [tokio-util](https://docs.rs/tokio-util)'s `Framed` with a codec over `Compat` |
| hyper's API in particular | `hyper::{client, server}::conn` over `hyper_util::rt::TokioIo::new(Compat::new(..))`; a server needs a timer, [see below](#hyper-servers-need-a-timer) |
| A crate that opens its own connections with Tokio (reqwest, tonic's `transport`, sqlx, most SDKs) | Not `Compat`: see below |

### What works

A crate works through `Compat` when **it takes the stream from you and you drive it**: a function such as `tokio_rustls::TlsConnector::connect(name, stream)`, `tokio_tungstenite::client_async(request, stream)`, `h2::client::handshake(stream)` or `hyper::client::conn::http1::handshake(io)`, which returns a future, or a connection object, that your task (or a task you start with `giong::spawn`) polls. Futures that are not `Send` are fine, since giong's tasks stay on their worker.

These are tested in [`tests/`](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.0.0-rc.1/giong-compat/tests), on giong's io_uring driver, its older ring setups and its epoll driver, with no Tokio runtime in the process:

| Crate | What the tests do |
|---|---|
| tokio-rustls 0.26 | A tokio-rustls client against a giong-tls server, and a giong-tls client against a tokio-rustls server (ALPN, `close_notify`), up to 1 MiB per message |
| futures-rustls 0.26 | A futures-rustls client (futures-io traits) against a giong-tls server |
| tokio-tungstenite 0.29 | A WebSocket echo server and client: text, a 4 MiB binary message, 1,000 messages queued before any is read, ping and pong, the close handshake |
| h2 0.4 | An HTTP/2 server and client: 100 streams at once on one connection with bodies over several flow-control windows; and h2 over giong-tls with ALPN `h2` |
| hyper 1 (HTTP/1) | hyper's client against a giong-http server, and giong-http's client against a hyper server, with keep-alive and bodies up to 500 KB; a hyper server with a timer on giong's timers closes a connection whose request head does not arrive in time |
| hyper 1 (HTTP/2) | hyper's client and server over `Compat`, with giong's tasks as hyper's executor: 100 requests at once on one connection, bodies up to 300 KB |
| tokio-util 0.7 | `LengthDelimitedCodec` over a Unix socket (200 frames up to 1 MB) and `LinesCodec` over TCP |

### What does not

`Compat` provides I/O traits, nothing else. A crate does not work through it when it

- **opens its own connections with `tokio::net`** (reqwest, tonic's `transport`, sqlx, redis-rs, most cloud SDKs): it panics with *"there is no reactor running, must be called from the context of a Tokio 1.x runtime"*, or never finishes;
- **uses Tokio's timers or spawns** (`tokio::time::sleep`, `tokio::time::timeout`, `tokio::spawn`): the same panic. hyper takes its timer and executor from you instead: see [hyper servers need a timer](#hyper-servers-need-a-timer);
- **requires `Send`** (bounds such as `T: Send` or `F: Future + Send + 'static`): `Compat` is not `Send`, because the stream belongs to one worker. The compiler says so.

Some of these crates take a custom connector or executor, and can work with one built on giong, but each has to be tried. Otherwise, run the crate on a Tokio runtime in a thread of its own.

### hyper servers need a timer

hyper's server enforces no timeout of its own: `header_read_timeout` needs a `hyper::rt::Timer`, and without one a client that sends half a request head and then nothing holds the connection, and the task serving it, for as long as it likes. Setting the timeout without a timer panics. giong's timers can back one:

```rust
use std::pin::Pin;
use std::task::{Context, Poll};
use std::time::{Duration, Instant};

/// hyper's timer, on giong's timers.
#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug)]
struct GiongTimer;

struct GiongSleep(giong::time::Sleep);

impl std::future::Future for GiongSleep {
    type Output = ();
    fn poll(mut self: Pin<&mut Self>, cx: &mut Context<'_>) -> Poll<()> {
        Pin::new(&mut self.0).poll(cx)
    }
}

impl hyper::rt::Sleep for GiongSleep {}

impl hyper::rt::Timer for GiongTimer {
    fn sleep(&self, duration: Duration) -> Pin<Box<dyn hyper::rt::Sleep>> {
        Box::pin(GiongSleep(giong::time::sleep(duration)))
    }
    fn sleep_until(&self, deadline: Instant) -> Pin<Box<dyn hyper::rt::Sleep>> {
        Box::pin(GiongSleep(giong::time::sleep_until(deadline)))
    }
}

// For each accepted connection:
// hyper::server::conn::http1::Builder::new()
//     .timer(GiongTimer)
//     .header_read_timeout(Duration::from_secs(10))
//     .serve_connection(hyper_util::rt::TokioIo::new(Compat::new(tcp)), service)
```

[`tests/hyper.rs`](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.0.0-rc.1/giong-compat/tests/hyper.rs) checks that a server built this way closes such a connection when the timeout ends.

hyper's HTTP/2, client and server, also takes an executor for the tasks it starts. They need not be `Send`, so giong's tasks do:

```rust
#[derive(Clone, Copy, Debug)]
struct GiongExec;

impl<F: std::future::Future + 'static> hyper::rt::Executor<F> for GiongExec {
    fn execute(&self, future: F) {
        giong::spawn(future);
    }
}

// hyper::server::conn::http2::Builder::new(GiongExec).timer(GiongTimer) ...
// hyper::client::conn::http2::handshake(GiongExec, io) ...
```

## How it behaves

- **Writes are buffered**, as with `BufWriter` or a TLS stream. `poll_write` copies the bytes and returns; they are sent on `flush`, when the buffer is full, or when a read on the same task is about to wait. Call `flush` (or `shutdown`) where the data must have gone out; every crate written for these traits does. A writer in another task than the reader must flush: a read only sends what its own task wrote. While one buffer is being sent the next one fills, so a long transfer keeps the socket busy.
- **The write buffer is bounded**: `Compat::new(stream).write_buffer(limit)`, 64 KiB by default, from 1 byte to 1 GiB (`GIONG-E1403` otherwise). A busy stream holds up to twice the limit; an idle one holds no buffer.
- **`TCP_NODELAY` is turned on** for TCP streams (plain or under TLS), as every giong crate does. `Compat` already gathers small writes until a flush, and Nagle's algorithm on top of that only delays them: the HTTP/2 test with 100 streams took 2.3 s with it and 21 ms without. `compat.get_ref().set_nodelay(false)` undoes it.
- **A failed send is reported by the next write, flush or shutdown**, with the kernel's own error (a large write sent straight to the socket reports its own failure at once); after that, writes, flushes and shutdowns fail with `GIONG-E1401`. So does a failed shutdown (a TLS stream that cannot send its `close_notify`). Writing after `shutdown` (or `close`) has started fails with `GIONG-E1402`. Reading still works in all these cases. A shutdown that finds the connection already reset counts as done, as with Tokio's `TcpStream`.
- **Dropping a `Compat` discards what was written but not flushed**, like dropping a `BufWriter`. Sends in flight are cancelled the way giong cancels any operation: their buffers stay alive until the kernel lets go.
- **One task reads and one task writes at a time.** `tokio::io::split` and `futures::io::AsyncReadExt::split` work, and so does splitting a `Framed` or a WebSocket stream.
- **Cancel safe.** A read that is dropped loses no data. A write either copies bytes and says how many, or copies nothing. [`tests/cancel.rs`](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.0.0-rc.1/giong-compat/tests/cancel.rs) drops reads, writes, flushes and whole streams at random (seeded, so a failure repeats), over TCP and giong-tls and through TLS 1.3 key updates, and checks every byte and that nothing leaks.
- **`fill_buf` holds a buffer of the worker's pool** until `consume` takes all of it, or a read or `consume` of part of it moves the rest to the heap. Do not wait on something else between `fill_buf` and `consume`: with many connections doing that, the worker's receive pool runs dry and every socket on the worker stalls. `consume` of more than `fill_buf` returned is ignored, as with std's and Tokio's `BufReader`.
- **Reading after the end of the stream** keeps returning 0 bytes. `into_inner().await` flushes and hands back the stream with the bytes received but not yet read, to go on with giong's own API.

## What it costs

giong reads into buffers from the worker's pool and writes buffers it owns until the kernel is done with them; these traits read into, and write from, memory the caller lends for one call. So `Compat` copies:

- **Reading:** each byte once more than giong's own `recv`, from the pool buffer into the caller's buffer. Through `AsyncBufRead` (`fill_buf`, then `consume` of the whole chunk) there is no extra copy. When a caller takes only part of a chunk, the rest moves to a heap buffer at once, so that a slow reader never holds on to the worker's pool.
- **Writing:** small writes are copied into the write buffer, which giong's `write_all` sends at a flush or when it fills; one small allocation per send (the future that sends it). A write at least as large as the buffer's limit (64 KiB by default), with nothing buffered or being sent before it, goes straight from the caller's memory to the socket in one `sendmsg(2)` that does not wait, as `BufWriter` and Tokio's streams do; only what the socket cannot take at once is copied.

Measured with [`bench/compat.sh`](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.0.0-rc.1/bench/compat.sh): one TCP stream over loopback, the measured side on one pinned core and the other end on another, the same peer for every variant, 9 runs interleaved. Median, with the range of the 9 runs in brackets. The machine is a 4-vCPU cloud VM (Xeon at 2.1 GHz, Linux 6.18), where bulk transfers over loopback vary from run to run and from one session to the next: read the medians, the spread, and the sessions below. This session (2026-11-17, [`bench/results/compat/`](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.0.0-rc.1/bench/results/compat/README.md)) ran this version, with giong's default receive buffers of 16 KiB (8 KiB until 0.8.0), and, interleaved, `Compat` from 0.8.0 on giong 0.8.0.

| Workload | giong's own API | `Compat` | `Compat` 0.8.0 | `Compat`, `AsyncBufRead` | Tokio |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Receive 2 GiB (peer writes 256 KiB at a time), MiB/s | 3124 [2876–3506] | 3197 [2946–3677] | 3503 [2703–4034] | 3280 [3045–3493] | 3041 [2479–3695] |
| CPU per KiB received | 139 ns | 147 ns | 170 ns | 141 ns | 124 ns |
| Send 2 GiB from a 64 KiB buffer, MiB/s | 2737 [2069–3196] | 2535 [2255–4642] | 2381 [2201–2553] | | 2404 [2266–3100] |
| CPU per KiB sent | 351 ns | 379 ns | 407 ns | | 404 ns |
| 64-byte request and reply, round trips/s | 33,815 [30,808–35,058] | 34,331 [31,586–35,290] | 33,159 [31,855–34,394] | | 34,194 [32,267–35,948] |
| CPU per round trip | 13.8 µs | 13.7 µs | 14.8 µs | | 14.0 µs |

Where `Compat` is behind Tokio, and why:

- **Receiving**, 19% more CPU per KiB with `read` and 14% with `AsyncBufRead` (30% and 17% in the session before, with 8 KiB receive buffers). Most of it is giong's own receive (12% above Tokio here): it receives into the worker's 16 KiB pool buffers, so 2 GiB take four times as many completions as Tokio's 64 KiB reads; 32 and 64 KiB pool buffers (`Builder::recv_buffers`) measured no better than 16 KiB. `read` then copies each byte once more into the caller's buffer, which `AsyncBufRead` avoids. Reading from the socket straight into the caller's buffer, as Tokio does, is not safe while giong's multishot receive is armed: data it has already taken could be handed out after data read later.

Where it is ahead: **sending**, 6% less CPU per KiB than Tokio in this session (7% less than 0.8.0's `Compat`; 9% and 2% more than Tokio in the two sessions before, on 8 KiB receive buffers, so read it as level), and **request and reply**, 2% less CPU per round trip than Tokio.

CPU is the measured thread's own (user and system, `CLOCK_THREAD_CPUTIME_ID`).

The cost of `Compat` moves from one session of 9 runs to the next by more than the difference it measures. Eight sessions on the same machine type, each the medians of 9 runs, `Compat` against giong's own API:

| Session (commit) | Send, MiB/s | Send, CPU per KiB | Receive with `read`, CPU per KiB | Receive with `AsyncBufRead`, CPU per KiB | Request and reply, round trips/s | CPU per round trip |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 (`f992163`) | −12.5% | +13.8% | +5.8% | −2.2% | −2.8% | +4.7% |
| 2 (`0bd788a`) | −16.1% | +19.4% | +11.8% | +3.9% | +1.2% | +3.4% |
| 3 (`0bd788a`) | −20.1% | +25.1% | +13.2% | +8.7% | −0.7% | +3.5% |
| 4 (`8632eb7`) | −10.3% | +14.6% | +13.1% | −4.6% | −1.9% | +1.4% |
| 5 (0.5.0 with #83) | +5.9% | −4.4% | +6.8% | −6.0% | +0.7% | +1.7% |
| 6 (0.5.0 with #83) | −4.3% | +4.6% | +15.8% | +4.4% | +0.7% | +1.9% |
| 7 (`8606db1` with #146) | −14.7% | +14.2% | +15.5% | +3.7% | −1.0% | +3.6% |
| 8 (this version, 16 KiB receive buffers, the table above) | −7.4% | +7.8% | +5.7% | +1.7% | +1.5% | −0.7% |

What the numbers say:

- **Sending** large writes now goes straight from the caller's memory to the socket (sessions 7 and 8). Until 0.8.0 each byte was copied into the write buffer first (under callgrind, `memcpy` was 96% of the user-space instructions `Compat` ran on this workload), which cost 10–20% of throughput and 14–25% more CPU per byte against giong's own `write_all` in sessions 1–4. In sessions 7 and 8 `Compat` sends at 5–7% less CPU per byte than 0.8.0's, from 9% above to 6% below Tokio. giong's own `write_all` measured faster than both (331 and 351 ns per KiB against Tokio's 347 and 404), which is why the column against it still shows +8% to +14%. Small writes are still gathered and copied: that is what lets `Compat` send one segment per flush.
- **Receiving** through `read` costs 6–16% more CPU per byte (5.7% in session 8) than giong's own `recv`, for the copy into the caller's buffer, at the same throughput. Through `AsyncBufRead` (`fill_buf`, then `consume`) there is no copy: the eight sessions put it between 6% below and 9% above giong's own cost, which is the noise between sessions.
- **Request and reply** differ by less than the noise in throughput; the CPU per round trip is up to 5% higher (0.7% lower in session 8). Callgrind counts about 1,000 more user-space instructions per round trip (the boxed send, the flush, one more poll), against 14 to 16 µs spent mostly in the kernel.
- **Tokio's own receive spends less CPU per KiB** than giong's `recv` on this benchmark: 11% less in session 8, with 16 KiB receive buffers, and 6–20% less in the sessions before, with 8 KiB. Each receive brings at most one buffer, so Tokio's 64 KiB reads take fewer system calls. That gap is giong's own, not `Compat`'s.

Run it with `bench/compat.sh` (the method is at the top of the script, and in [`bench/compat/src/main.rs`](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.0.0-rc.1/bench/compat/src/main.rs)); the raw numbers of the latest session are in [`bench/results/compat/`](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.0.0-rc.1/bench/results/compat), the earlier ones in its `sessions/` folder.

## Errors

| Code | When |
|---|---|
| [`GIONG-E1401`](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.0.0-rc.1/docs/errors/E1401.md) | A write, flush or shutdown after a buffered send or a shutdown failed (the first call after the failure got the error itself) |
| [`GIONG-E1402`](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.0.0-rc.1/docs/errors/E1402.md) | A write after `shutdown` or `close` started |
| [`GIONG-E1403`](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.0.0-rc.1/docs/errors/E1403.md) | `write_buffer` given 0 or more than 1 GiB (a panic) |

`giong::error::code(&err)` returns the code, to match on instead of the message.

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.0.0-rc.1/examples/rest-api/README.md -->

# rest-api

A complete REST API on giong: users kept in PostgreSQL, read through a Redis cache, served over HTTPS. Every piece is a giong crate ([`giong-web`](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.0.0-rc.1/giong-web/README.md), [`giong-postgres`](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.0.0-rc.1/giong-postgres/README.md), [`giong-redis`](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.0.0-rc.1/giong-redis/README.md), [`giong-tls`](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.0.0-rc.1/giong-tls/README.md)); nothing comes from the Tokio ecosystem.

```sh
openssl req -x509 -newkey ec -pkeyopt ec_paramgen_curve:prime256v1 -nodes \
  -keyout key.pem -out cert.pem -days 30 -subj "/CN=localhost" \
  -addext "subjectAltName=DNS:localhost" -addext "basicConstraints=critical,CA:FALSE"
DATABASE_URL=postgres://app:secret@localhost/app REDIS_URL=redis://127.0.0.1:6379 \
  TLS_CERT=cert.pem TLS_KEY=key.pem cargo run --release -p rest-api

curl -k https://localhost:8443/users -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"name":"Ada Lovelace","email":"ada@example.com"}'
# {"id":1,"name":"Ada Lovelace","email":"ada@example.com","created_at":"2026-11-13T11:02:41.318402Z"}
curl -k https://localhost:8443/users/1 -i    # X-Cache: miss, then hit
```

| Route | What it does |
|---|---|
| `GET /health` | `ok` while the process runs |
| `GET /ready` | `ready` when PostgreSQL and Redis answer, `503` otherwise |
| `GET /users?limit=50&after=0` | a page of users by id (`limit` 1 to 1000), and the `after` of the next page |
| `POST /users` | creates a user: `201` with `Location`; `409` `email_taken`; `422` `invalid_name` or `invalid_email` |
| `GET /users/{id}` | one user, from Redis when it is there (`X-Cache: hit`), from PostgreSQL otherwise (`miss`, then cached) |
| `PUT /users/{id}` | replaces the name and email, and drops the cached copy |
| `DELETE /users/{id}` | `204`, and drops the cached copy |
| `GET /users/export` | every user as NDJSON, read 1,000 rows at a time and streamed |

Errors are problem+json bodies with a code (`{"status":404,"code":"user_not_found","title":"Not Found","detail":"no user has the id 9","request_id":"..."}`). A database or cache that cannot be reached gives `503` with `Retry-After`, its cause in the log only.

## Configuration

| Variable | Default | |
|---|---|---|
| `DATABASE_URL` | (required) | `postgres://user:password@host/db`; TLS to a remote host is on and verified by default |
| `REDIS_URL` | `redis://127.0.0.1:6379` | `rediss://` for TLS, `redis+unix:///path` for a socket |
| `LISTEN` | `0.0.0.0:8443` | |
| `TLS_CERT`, `TLS_KEY` | (none) | PEM files; without both, plain HTTP (behind a proxy that does TLS) |
| `WORKERS` | every core | |
| `DB_POOL`, `CACHE_POOL` | `2`, `1` | connections per worker: statements and commands pipeline over them, so a few go a long way |
| `CACHE_TTL_SECS` | `60` | |
| `ACCESS_LOG` | `stdout` | one JSON line per request, or `off` |

The table is created at startup when it is missing. SIGTERM and SIGINT stop accepting, answer the requests in progress (for up to 10 s) and exit.

## How it is built

- `src/lib.rs` is the API: the handlers and `app(state, log)`, which the test builds too. `src/main.rs` reads the environment, creates the table once, then starts one worker per core.
- Each worker has its own pools, app and listener: nothing is shared between threads and nothing is locked. The kernel spreads connections over the workers' listeners.
- Reads are cache-aside: Redis first, then PostgreSQL, then the row is cached for `CACHE_TTL_SECS`. A Redis that is down slows reads down but does not fail them. Writes delete the cached copy after the database has changed, so a read in between caches at most the old row until it expires.
- Middleware: request ids, the JSON-line access log, gzip from 1 KiB, and a 10 s timeout. Request bodies are refused past 64 KiB.
- `GET /users/export` writes its body with `Body::channel`: one page in memory at a time, whatever the table's size, and a client that reads slowly slows the reading down.

## Tests

`cargo test -p rest-api` starts a throwaway PostgreSQL cluster and Redis server (both on Unix sockets in a temporary directory), serves the API over HTTPS on a free port, and goes through every route with giong-http's client: create, conflict, validation, cache miss then hit, update and the cache dropped, pages, the export, delete, and reads that still work with the cache unreachable while `/ready` says `503`. Without PostgreSQL or Redis installed the test is skipped, unless `GIONG_PG_REQUIRED=1` or `GIONG_REDIS_REQUIRED=1`.

`cargo test -p rest-api --doc` compiles the Rust samples in the repository's READMEs, `docs/DEPLOYMENT.md` and `docs/errors/README.md` against the crates as they are, and runs the ones that need no server, database or certificate, so that no sample drifts from the API.

## Against axum

[`bench/rest-api-axum`](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.0.0-rc.1/bench/rest-api-axum) is the same API on axum 0.8, tokio-postgres with deadpool-postgres, redis-rs and rustls: the same routes, SQL, validation, cache and middleware. `bench/rest-api.sh` measures both; see [Performance](#performance).

## Performance

Measured with `bench/rest-api.sh`: this example against the same API on axum 0.8.9 (Tokio 1.54, tokio-postgres 0.7.18 with deadpool-postgres 0.14.2, redis-rs 1.8.1, rustls 0.23.46 through axum-server 0.7.3, tower-http 0.6.11), on a 4-vCPU virtual machine (Xeon 2.1 GHz, Linux 6.18). Each server runs one worker on its own core and serves HTTPS (TLS 1.3, a P-256 certificate); `wrk` 4.1 runs on a second core with 50 connections; PostgreSQL 16.15 (with `fsync` off, so writes measure the servers and not the disk) and Redis 7.0.15 share the last two, with 10,000 users. `get` reads one of the first 1,000 users, from the cache; `list` reads a page of 20 from PostgreSQL; `create` inserts a user. Neither writes an access log; both add request ids, gzip and the 10 s timeout. giong keeps 2 PostgreSQL connections, axum 32, its best in a sweep of 4, 8, 16, 32 and 64. Requests per second, median of 5 interleaved rounds of 5 s, with the range; p99 is the median of the rounds' p99s. Every response was a 2xx.

| | `get` (cache) | p99 | `list` (PostgreSQL) | p99 | `create` | p99 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **giong** | **65.7k** (60.0–71.6k) | **2.22 ms** | **28.2k** (25.8–36.1k) | **4.11 ms** | **47.7k** (46.9–48.5k) | **3.78 ms** |
| axum | 43.6k (41.8–44.6k) | 3.39 ms | 18.1k (16.9–18.8k) | 7.74 ms | 23.6k (21.2–26.6k) | 5.91 ms |

- **1.5 times axum on cached reads, 1.6 times on pages from PostgreSQL, 2.0 times on inserts.**
- The server's core was what limited every run: 94 to 97% busy for both. On `list`, giong kept the two database cores 179% busy out of 200, axum 171%.
- Resident memory, read after each measurement: 8.1 to 8.4 MiB for giong, 9.2 to 9.5 MiB for axum. Of giong's 8.4 MiB, about 3.1 MiB are the pages of its own code, 2.2 MiB those of libc and the other shared libraries, and 2.9 MiB its data; heaptrack puts the peak of the heap under this load at 2.2 MiB, of which about 0.5 MiB are buffers and future blocks kept for reuse.

Not measured yet: several workers, `PUT`, `DELETE` and the export, and the access log on. Results are in `bench/results/rest-api/`.

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.0.0-rc.1/docs/DEPLOYMENT.md -->

# Deploying giong

giong is fastest on io_uring, which needs Linux 6.0 or newer (6.1 or newer recommended)
and the three io_uring system calls: `io_uring_setup`, `io_uring_enter` and
`io_uring_register`. Many container platforms block them by default.

Where io_uring cannot be used, giong runs on its **epoll driver** instead, without being
told: in a Docker container with the default seccomp profile, in Kubernetes with the
`RuntimeDefault` profile, under gVisor, with the `kernel.io_uring_disabled` sysctl set,
on a kernel older than 6.0, or on Linux 6.14 to 7.2 when the
[locked-memory limit](#locked-memory-limit) is used up. Every API works the same way on
both drivers; epoll makes more system calls per request, and file operations run on a
pool of blocking threads.
When giong falls back by itself it says so once on stderr, with the reason (the same
`GIONG-E…` error a runtime that insists on io_uring would get). `giong::driver_choice()`
tells which driver a worker got, who chose it, and why io_uring is not used; log it at
startup:

```rust
giong::block_on(async {
    eprintln!("giong driver: {}", giong::driver_choice());
    // io_uring (chosen automatically)
});
```

`giong-mcp`'s `overview` shows the same for each worker. The
[README](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.0.0-rc.1/README.md#two-drivers-io_uring-and-epoll) has the measured difference.

So a container needs no special settings to run giong. Allow io_uring, as this page shows,
when you want its speed:

- `Builder::driver(DriverKind::IoUring)`, or `GIONG_DRIVER=io_uring` in the environment,
  makes the runtime fail to start where io_uring is blocked, instead of running on epoll.
  The error begins with `giong needs io_uring, which is not available here`
  ([GIONG-E0001](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.0.0-rc.1/docs/errors/E0001.md)).
- `Builder::driver(DriverKind::Epoll)`, or `GIONG_DRIVER=epoll`, uses epoll even where
  io_uring is available.

## Check a machine

```sh
uname -r                              # 6.0 or newer
cat /proc/sys/kernel/io_uring_disabled  # Linux 6.6+: 0 = allowed
ulimit -l                             # Linux 6.14-7.2: unlimited, or 150 KiB per worker
```

`kernel.io_uring_disabled` (Linux 6.6 and newer): `0` allows io_uring for every process,
`1` only for privileged processes and members of the group in `kernel.io_uring_group`,
`2` for nobody. Set it with `sysctl -w kernel.io_uring_disabled=0`, or put the service's
user in that group.

## Locked-memory limit

Linux 6.14 to 7.2 count the memory of every io_uring ring against the locked-memory limit
(`RLIMIT_MEMLOCK`, `ulimit -l`) of a process that lacks `CAP_IPC_LOCK`. Linux 7.3 stopped,
and so did 6.18 from 6.18.58; distribution kernels may have taken the change too. The
count is kept per user ID and summed over all of that user's processes, and the memory of
a closed ring is given back a moment after the close. A giong worker locks about 150 KiB
with the default settings: the submission and completion queues take 136 KiB of it
(`Builder::ring_entries`), the two rings of receive buffers 8 KiB each
(`Builder::recv_buffers`). The usual default limit of 8 MiB holds about fifty workers, for
all of the user's processes together; the 64 KiB of older systems holds none.

A worker that cannot lock the memory gets `ENOMEM` from the kernel, which giong reports as
[GIONG-E0010](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.0.0-rc.1/docs/errors/E0010.md), naming the limit; without an explicit driver it runs that
worker on epoll and says so once on stderr. Root is not held to the limit, since it has
`CAP_IPC_LOCK`, except where that capability was taken away, as in a Docker container.
Raise the limit, or lift it, for any service that is not root:

- systemd: `LimitMEMLOCK=infinity` in the `[Service]` section, or
  `AmbientCapabilities=CAP_IPC_LOCK` to lift it for a service with a `User=`.
- Docker: `docker run --ulimit memlock=-1:-1`, or in Docker Compose:

  ```yaml
  services:
    api:
      ulimits:
        memlock:
          soft: -1
          hard: -1
  ```

- Kubernetes has no setting for the limit. Add the capability where the pod's security
  policy allows it (`securityContext.capabilities.add: ["IPC_LOCK"]`; Pod Security's
  `baseline` and `restricted` levels do not), or raise the limit the container runtime
  starts containers with on each node (for containerd, `LimitMEMLOCK=infinity` in a
  drop-in for its systemd unit). Containers that run as the same user ID on one node share
  the count.
- A shell: `ulimit -l unlimited` as root before starting the service, or an entry in
  `/etc/security/limits.conf` for its user.

Or need less: fewer workers, a smaller `Builder::ring_entries`, fewer receive buffers. Or
run a kernel that does not count the rings.

## Ubuntu 24.04

Ubuntu's 6.8 kernels from 6.8.0-135 on have a bug that makes them refuse every correctly
formed io_uring buffer ring, which giong's io_uring driver needs: a backport inverted a
check on the request's reserved fields. The AWS, Azure, GCP and Oracle 6.8 kernels built
from them have it too, as does the 6.8 HWE kernel of Ubuntu 22.04. giong recognises the bug and registers its ring
the way those kernels accept, so io_uring works there at full speed, and
`giong::driver_choice()` lists the workaround (`buffer-ring-reserved-check`). Nothing to
do on your side. Other software that uses buffer rings through liburing fails on those
kernels with `EINVAL`. The 7.0 HWE kernel (`linux-generic-hwe-24.04`) does not have the
bug.

## Linux 6.0.16 to 6.0.19

The last four releases of the 6.0 series (which is no longer maintained) return 1
instead of -1 from bind(2) on a TCP socket whose address is in use, and leave the socket
unbound. Programs read that as success, and listen(2) then puts the socket on a free port
of every interface, so a server asked for a busy port starts on another one.
`giong::net::TcpListener::bind` checks which port the socket ended up on and fails with
`AddrInUse`, as on every other kernel. A listener that the standard library bound, handed
over with `TcpListener::from_std`, is not checked: compare its `local_addr()` with the
address you asked for, or let giong bind it. 6.0.15 and older, 6.1 and later, and UDP and
Unix sockets are not affected.

## Restarting on the same port

`TcpListener::bind`, `bind_balanced` and `UdpSocket::bind` let the workers of one process
share a port, and refuse it, with `AddrInUse`, while a socket of another process holds
it: a service started twice by mistake fails the second time instead of quietly taking
half of the first one's connections. What that means for a restart:

- Stopping the old process before starting the new one (systemd's `Restart=`, a container
  replaced by its orchestrator) needs nothing: the port of a closed listener can be bound
  again at once.
- Starting the new version on the same machine and port while the old one still serves
  fails until the old one has let the port go. Run the two on different ports behind the
  load balancer or proxy, or create the sockets outside giong: one per worker, with
  `SO_REUSEPORT` set (with the `socket2` crate, say) by every process that is to share the
  port, wrapped with `TcpListener::from_std` or `UdpSocket::from_std` in each worker.
  giong sets no option on such a socket and does not check who else holds its port.
- Connections still in a closing listener's accept queue are refused when it closes: have
  the load balancer stop sending to the old process first, and give it a
  `Builder::shutdown_grace` to answer what it already has.

## Sizing memory

What a giong-http server holds is bounded by its settings, per worker (each worker runs its
own `serve`):

```text
memory per worker  ≈  max_buffered_request_bytes
                    + open connections × (idle cost + up to 4 KiB while a request arrives)
                    + what the handlers hold
```

- `max_buffered_request_bytes` bounds the requests the worker is receiving in full: by
  default 64 MiB, or a quarter of the cgroup memory limit divided among the workers if that
  is less, so that one worker in a 128 MiB container takes 32 MiB at most. Past it, requests
  are refused with `503` (HTTP/1.1) or `REFUSED_STREAM` (HTTP/2) instead of being buffered
  ([GIONG-E1120](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.0.0-rc.1/docs/errors/E1120.md)). Bodies read as a stream (`Handler::stream_body`) hold
  one piece at a time and are not counted.
- An idle connection costs about 2 KiB over HTTP/1.1, 4.5 KiB over HTTP/2 and 10.5 KiB over
  HTTPS in the process, and the kernel about 4 KiB more per socket (charged to the
  container's memory under cgroup v2). `max_connections` (10,000 per `serve` call by
  default) bounds the count.

The defaults fit the budget to the container, but not the number of connections: 10,000
idle HTTPS connections take about 145 MiB with the kernel's share. Past what fits, the
server does not get killed: while less than `min_free_memory` is left to the process (a
tenth of the container's limit by default, between 16 and 256 MiB), it refuses new
connections with `503` and `Retry-After: 1`, or closes them before the TLS handshake
([GIONG-E1121](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.0.0-rc.1/docs/errors/E1121.md)), and keeps serving the ones it holds. That is a last line
of defence, which refuses clients the load balancer could have sent elsewhere. In a small
container, lower `max_connections` to what fits next to the budget, so that the server
stops accepting before memory runs low:

```rust
use giong_http::Server;

// One worker in a 256 MiB container, serving HTTPS: 64 MiB for requests being
// received, 5,000 connections x ~17 KiB = 83 MiB, and the rest for the program.
let server = Server::new()
    .max_buffered_request_bytes(64 << 20)
    .max_connections(5_000);
```

CI checks the bound: the `slow-uploads` job runs a server with one worker and with four in
a Docker container limited to 128 MiB, sends it hundreds of uploads that stop one byte short
of their announced length, over HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2, and fails if the container is
OOM-killed or a well-behaved client mixed in stops getting answers
([scripts/slow-uploads.sh](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.0.0-rc.1/scripts/slow-uploads.sh)). The same job then runs it in 48 MiB
and opens idle connections until it refuses them, and fails if the container is
OOM-killed, if the connections it holds stop being served, or if it does not take new ones
once those close ([scripts/idle-connections.sh](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.0.0-rc.1/scripts/idle-connections.sh)).

## Docker

Docker's default seccomp profile does not allow the io_uring system calls, so in a
container run with default settings giong uses its epoll driver. For io_uring, use a
profile that is Docker's default plus those three calls:

```sh
curl -fsSLo docker-default.json \
  https://raw.githubusercontent.com/moby/profiles/main/seccomp/default.json
jq '.syscalls += [{"names": ["io_uring_setup", "io_uring_enter", "io_uring_register"],
                   "action": "SCMP_ACT_ALLOW"}]' docker-default.json > giong-seccomp.json

docker run --security-opt seccomp=giong-seccomp.json your-image
```

With Docker Compose:

```yaml
services:
  api:
    image: your-image
    security_opt:
      - seccomp=giong-seccomp.json
```

This keeps every other restriction of the default profile. Avoid
`--security-opt seccomp=unconfined`, which turns all of them off.

Checked on Docker Engine 29.9.2 with a static binary that starts a runtime and does a TCP
round trip: with `giong-seccomp.json` it runs on io_uring. With the default profile,
giong's test suite runs on the epoll driver in CI (the `docker` job).

## Kubernetes

A pod's containers get the container runtime's default profile when their
`securityContext.seccompProfile.type` is `RuntimeDefault`, and also by default on
kubelets started with `--seccomp-default`. Pod Security's `restricted` level requires
either `RuntimeDefault` or `Localhost`. containerd's default profile blocks io_uring like Docker's does.

Install `giong-seccomp.json` from above on every node, under the kubelet's seccomp
directory (by default `/var/lib/kubelet/seccomp/`), for example as
`profiles/giong.json`, and point the container at it:

```yaml
securityContext:
  seccompProfile:
    type: Localhost
    localhostProfile: profiles/giong.json
```

The [Security Profiles Operator](https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/security-profiles-operator)
can distribute the profile to the nodes for you. Managed platforms differ in what they
let you change; check that yours allows `Localhost` profiles.

## Sandboxes

Runtimes that put a user-space kernel between the container and Linux, such as gVisor
(used by GKE Sandbox), do not offer io_uring by default. giong runs on epoll there; run it
outside such a sandbox for io_uring.

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.0.0-rc.1/docs/errors/README.md -->

# Error codes

Every error giong raises itself starts with a code and ends with a link to its page here:

```text
GIONG-E0102: no address found for db.internal. Fix: check the spelling of the name,
/etc/hosts, and the DNS servers in /etc/resolv.conf (in a container, the network it is
attached to). See https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/main/docs/errors/E0102.md
```

Errors giong only passes on, such as "connection refused" from the kernel, have no code.
Functions still return `std::io::Error`; match on the code, not on the message:

```rust
use giong::error::{self, Code};

fn on_error(err: &std::io::Error) {
    if error::code(err) == Some(Code::HostNotFound) {
        // ...
    }
}
```

giong-http, giong-web, giong-tls, giong-postgres, giong-mysql, giong-redis, giong-mcp and
giong-compat use the same codes. A code is never reused or renumbered, and its page stays
when it is no longer raised.

| [GIONG-E3109](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.0.0-rc.1/docs/errors/E3109.md) | `MysqlPoolTimeout` | MySQL pool wait timed out |

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.0.0-rc.1/docs/errors/E0001.md -->

# GIONG-E0001: io_uring is not available

Raised by the runtime, when a worker starts. In code: `giong::error::Code::IoUringUnavailable`.

## What happened

The runtime was told to use io_uring (`Builder::driver(DriverKind::IoUring)`, or `GIONG_DRIVER=io_uring`), and `io_uring_setup` failed with `EPERM`, `EACCES` or `ENOSYS`. The kernel has io_uring but this process may not use it, or the kernel (or a sandbox in front of it) does not have it at all. Without that instruction giong would have used its epoll driver instead. The error keeps the kernel's `io::ErrorKind` (`PermissionDenied` or `Unsupported`), and the kernel's error is its `source()`.

## How to fix it

- If epoll is good enough here, stop asking for io_uring: remove `.driver(DriverKind::IoUring)` and unset `GIONG_DRIVER`, and giong falls back to epoll by itself.
- In Docker, the default seccomp profile blocks io_uring. Run with a profile that allows `io_uring_setup`, `io_uring_enter` and `io_uring_register` (see [DEPLOYMENT.md](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.0.0-rc.1/docs/DEPLOYMENT.md)), or `--security-opt seccomp=unconfined` to confirm that this is the cause.
- In Kubernetes, the container runtime applies the same default profile: set a `seccompProfile` of type `Localhost` that allows the three calls, as [DEPLOYMENT.md](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.0.0-rc.1/docs/DEPLOYMENT.md) shows.
- On the host, `sysctl kernel.io_uring_disabled` must be `0`, or `1` with the process in the group named by `kernel.io_uring_group`.
- gVisor and some other sandboxes do not offer io_uring by default; run giong outside them.

[All error codes](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.0.0-rc.1/docs/errors/README.md)

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.0.0-rc.1/docs/errors/E0002.md -->

# GIONG-E0002: the kernel is too old

Raised by the runtime, when a worker starts. In code: `giong::error::Code::KernelTooOld`.

## What happened

The runtime was told to use io_uring (`Builder::driver(DriverKind::IoUring)`, or `GIONG_DRIVER=io_uring`), and the kernel is missing an io_uring feature giong needs: registering a ring of receive buffers (`IORING_REGISTER_PBUF_RING`) failed. It arrived in Linux 5.19 and works reliably from 6.0, the oldest kernel giong's io_uring driver supports. Without that instruction giong would have used its epoll driver, which works on older kernels.

## How to fix it

- If epoll is good enough here, stop asking for io_uring: remove `.driver(DriverKind::IoUring)` and unset `GIONG_DRIVER`.
- Run on Linux 6.0 or newer; 6.1 or newer is faster (giong then uses `IORING_SETUP_DEFER_TASKRUN`). `uname -r` shows the version.
- On a managed platform, pick a node image with a newer kernel.

[All error codes](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.0.0-rc.1/docs/errors/README.md)

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.0.0-rc.1/docs/errors/E0003.md -->

# GIONG-E0003: another runtime handles the signals

Raised by the runtime, when it starts. In code: `giong::error::Code::SignalsTaken`.

## What happened

The runtime was built with `Builder::shutdown_on_signals(true)`, but another giong runtime in this process already handles `SIGINT` and `SIGTERM`. Signal handlers belong to the whole process, so only one runtime at a time can own them.

## How to fix it

- Turn on `shutdown_on_signals` for one runtime only, and stop the others through their `Handle::shutdown`.
- Or run one runtime at a time: the handlers are released when that runtime's `run` returns.

[All error codes](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.0.0-rc.1/docs/errors/README.md)

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.0.0-rc.1/docs/errors/E0004.md -->

# GIONG-E0004: invalid runtime setting

Raised by the runtime, when it starts. In code: `giong::error::Code::InvalidConfig`.

## What happened

A runtime setting is outside the range giong accepts, such as the number or the size of the receive buffers, or the `GIONG_DRIVER` environment variable names no driver.

## How to fix it

- Read the message: it names the setting, the range and the value given.
- `Builder::recv_buffers(count, size)` takes up to 32768 buffers, rounded up to a power of two, and a size from 64 bytes to 4 GiB.
- `GIONG_DRIVER` takes `io_uring` or `epoll`; unset or empty (or `auto`) means io_uring where the kernel allows it and epoll elsewhere. It is read only when the code does not call `Builder::driver`.

[All error codes](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.0.0-rc.1/docs/errors/README.md)

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.0.0-rc.1/docs/errors/E0005.md -->

# GIONG-E0005: unexpected result from the kernel

Raised by the runtime's I/O operations, and as a panic that stops the worker when its event loop gets an error it cannot go on after (from `io_uring_enter` or `epoll_wait`). In code: `giong::error::Code::Unexpected`.

## What happened

The kernel returned something giong does not expect, such as received data without a buffer or a datagram from an unknown address family. It points to a bug in giong or in the kernel, with one exception: a panic naming `EBADR` or `ENOMEM` means the kernel ran out of memory and dropped completions, after which the worker cannot know which operations finished.

## How to fix it

- If the message names `EBADR` or `ENOMEM`: give the process more memory, or run fewer connections per worker.
- Otherwise, please report it at https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/issues with the message, your kernel version (`uname -r`) and, if you can, a way to reproduce it.
- Running the same program on another kernel version helps tell the two apart.

[All error codes](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.0.0-rc.1/docs/errors/README.md)

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.0.0-rc.1/docs/errors/E0006.md -->

# GIONG-E0006: read used after recv

Raised by `TcpStream`, `UnixStream` and `UdpSocket`. In code: `giong::error::Code::MixedReads`.

## What happened

A one-off read (`read`, `read_from`) was used on a stream or socket that already has a multishot receive (`recv`, `recv_from`) running. The kernel keeps delivering data into the multishot receive, so a one-off read would see the data out of order.

## How to fix it

- Use one way of reading per stream or socket: `recv`/`recv_from` (buffers from the runtime's pool, best for many connections) or `read`/`read_from` (your own buffer).

[All error codes](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.0.0-rc.1/docs/errors/README.md)

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.0.0-rc.1/docs/errors/E0007.md -->

# GIONG-E0007: the time limit passed

Raised by `giong::time::timeout`, when its error becomes an `io::Error`. In code: `giong::error::Code::TimedOut`.

## What happened

The future given to `giong::time::timeout` did not finish within its time limit, and the `Elapsed` error was turned into an `io::Error` (by `?` in a function returning `io::Result`). The future was dropped, which cancels its I/O.

## How to fix it

- Give it more time if the limit is too tight for the work.
- Otherwise find out why the operation is slow: the peer, the network, or a task that keeps the worker busy (one worker runs every task on its core).

[All error codes](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.0.0-rc.1/docs/errors/README.md)

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.0.0-rc.1/docs/errors/E0008.md -->

# GIONG-E0008: no such worker

Raised by `giong::Handle::spawn_on`, as a panic. In code: `giong::error::Code::NoSuchWorker`.

## What happened

`spawn_on` was given a worker index that the runtime does not have. Workers are numbered from 0 to `Handle::workers() - 1`. This is a bug in the calling code, so `spawn_on` panics instead of returning an error.

## How to fix it

- Pass an index below `Handle::workers()`. To spread work over every worker, use `i % handle.workers()`.
- `Builder::workers` sets the count; without it, the runtime starts one worker for each CPU the process may run on, which differs between machines and containers.

[All error codes](https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.0.0-rc.1/docs/errors/README.md)

---

<!-- https://github.com/giong-run/Giong/blob/v1.0.0-rc.1/docs/errors/E0009.md -->

# GIONG-E0009: the kernel refused io_uring buffer rings

Raised by the runtime, when a worker starts. In code: `giong::error::Code::BufferRingRefused`.

## What happened

The runtime was told to use io_uring (`Builder::driver(DriverKind::IoUring)`, or `GIONG_DRIVER=io_uring`), the kernel is 6.0 or newer, and it would not register giong's ring of receive buffers (`IORING_REGISTER_PBUF_RING`). Such a kernel should accept it, and giong already works around the kernel bugs it knows here, such as the inverted check in Ubuntu's 6.8.0-135 and later kernels (`giong::KernelWorkaround`). The message names the kernel release, the kernel's error is the `source()`, and its `io::ErrorKind` is kept. Without that instruction giong would have used its epoll driver.

## How to fix it

- If epoll is good enough here, stop asking for io_uring: remove `.driver(DriverKind::IoUring)` and unset `GIONG_DRIVER`. `giong::driver_choice()` then reports this same error as the reason giong chose epoll.
- `ENOMEM` means the memory for the ring could not be had: check the service's memory cgroup limit, or give it fewer receive buffers (`Builder::recv_buffers`).
